claims.claim: Ordway notes Lions comes full circle by ending on the reaction of Alvar, one of the first characters introduced.
claims.source: Holly E. Ordway, 'The World-Building of Guy Gavriel Kay' (UMass Amherst independent study, 1998; presented at the 1998 Academic Conference on Canadian SF&F)
claims.quote: the novel also comes full circle

claims.claim: Ordway quotes the surgery passage that opens 'what happened that night... became legendary', a retrospective legend-framing of an event.
claims.source: Holly E. Ordway, 'The World-Building of Guy Gavriel Kay' (UMass Amherst independent study, 1998; presented at the 1998 Academic Conference on Canadian SF&F)

claims.claim: Gunn identifies Tigana's flavour as facing up to consequences other fantasy glosses over, e.g. the enslaved wizard's protest.
claims.source: James Gunn, 'The Other Side of the Mirror: Tigana' (introduction to the Easton Press edition, 1998)
claims.quote: facing-up to the consequences of actions glossed over

claims.claim: Gunn says Tigana reads like a richly tapestried historical novel dense with character and detail.
claims.source: James Gunn, 'The Other Side of the Mirror: Tigana' (introduction to the Easton Press edition, 1998)
claims.quote: richly tapestried historical novel dense with character and detail

claims.claim: Gunn notes Kay's willingness to kill off attractive major characters gives an edge of reality.
claims.source: James Gunn, 'The Other Side of the Mirror: Tigana' (introduction to the Easton Press edition, 1998)
claims.quote: his willingness to kill off major characters

claims.claim: Gunn quotes Kuzca's Encyclopedia of Fantasy entry that Kay attempts a grittier, harsher world than is common within fantasy, and speculates TV work taught scene-setting and dialogue.
claims.source: James Gunn, 'The Other Side of the Mirror: Tigana' (introduction to the Easton Press edition, 1998)
claims.quote: grittier, harsher world than is common within fantasy

claims.claim: Malosse notes the 1300-page Mosaic has many characters and narrative points of view, making summary difficult.
claims.source: Pierre-Louis Malosse, 'Justinien visité et revisité', Anabases 5 (2007) 229-235, English translation by Morgon Mills
claims.quote: many characters and many narrative points of view

claims.claim: Malosse credits Kay with giving characters the knowledge, conceits and superstitions of the time; anachronisms are of nuance not fact.
claims.source: Pierre-Louis Malosse, 'Justinien visité et revisité', Anabases 5 (2007) 229-235, English translation by Morgon Mills
claims.quote: the knowledge and the conceits of the time

claims.claim: Malosse argues the deliberately unfaithful Sarantium evokes Late Antiquity more exactly than de Camp's or Silverberg's respectful time-travel novels.
claims.source: Pierre-Louis Malosse, 'Justinien visité et revisité', Anabases 5 (2007) 229-235, English translation by Morgon Mills
claims.quote: Its false Byzantium is more real

claims.claim: Malosse lists the transparent substitutions (Rhodias/Rome, Varena/Ravenna, Pertennius/Procopius) as an undisguised debt.
claims.source: Pierre-Louis Malosse, 'Justinien visité et revisité', Anabases 5 (2007) 229-235, English translation by Morgon Mills
claims.quote: under the new names – often transparent

claims.claim: Malosse chooses Alixana's porphyry-shroud speech, narrated as a senator's later memory, to exemplify Kay's style against Procopius's account.
claims.source: Pierre-Louis Malosse, 'Justinien visité et revisité', Anabases 5 (2007) 229-235, English translation by Morgon Mills
claims.quote: as compared with the narrative supplied by Procopius

claims.feature: resolution by action and historical whim
claims.claim: Taylor notes Lions resolves outcomes by both individual action and the whims of history, magic and heroism alone being precluded.
claims.source: Dena Taylor, 'Three Glasses of Wine: The Accommodation of Culture in The Lions of Al-Rassan' (Babel Handbooks/Nimrod Press chapter)
claims.quote: both individual action and the whims of history

claims.claim: Taylor reads the epilogue's three full glasses of wine left standing together as the novel's culminating image.
claims.source: Dena Taylor, 'Three Glasses of Wine: The Accommodation of Culture in The Lions of Al-Rassan' (Babel Handbooks/Nimrod Press chapter)
claims.quote: Three full glasses of wine, intentionally left standing together

claims.claim: Taylor documents that the Sarantine titles and vision derive from Yeats's Byzantium poems and that the title phrase is an in-world idiom for a life at a cusp.
claims.source: Dena Taylor, 'On Sailing to Sarantium', TransVersions 10 (1999)

claims.claim: Hatch argues the non-chronological, flashback-laden, multi-focalized narrative creates a sense of cause and effect in history rather than a timeline.
claims.source: Jillian Hatch, 'The Creative Construction of History in Guy Gavriel Kay's The Sarantine Mosaic' (University of Calgary undergraduate paper, 2005)
claims.quote: creates a sense of cause and effect in history
